faqs.q: When can bats be removed from a Summerville home?
faqs.a: Bat work here is exclusion only, and no permit is required to remove bats in South Carolina. What controls the timing is SCDNR guidance, which we follow: complete exclusions are planned for early spring (March-April) or fall (August-October), and we do not run a full exclusion from May through mid-July, sometimes into August, because flightless pups would be trapped inside. That window is agency guidance, not a state law. We can inspect and map every entry at any time of year, and a bat found inside your living space is different — keep the room closed and call us, because bats in living quarters are a rabies-testing situation handled with the Department of Public Health.

faqs.q: Are armadillos really established around Summerville?
faqs.a: Yes. Nine-banded armadillos are established throughout the entirety of South Carolina, and around here they burrow under porches, driveways, and crawlspace edges and root up lawns hunting grubs and worms. We trap the animals working your property and backfill and screen the burrow openings, because an open burrow in this soil is quickly claimed by the next armadillo — or by a skunk or opossum.

faqs.q: How much does wildlife removal cost in Summerville?
faqs.a: It depends on the structure and the species — a single squirrel entry on a newer subdivision home is one job, while a bat colony across a historic roofline with six junctions is another. We inspect first and give you a firm quote before work starts, and the inspection covers the whole building: attic, chimney, and the canopy contacts, so the number is the complete job. Removal runs under a depredation permit issued for your property, and we are glad to walk through what that covers when we quote.

faqs.q: Bats are in our historic Summerville attic in June. When can they be excluded?
faqs.a: As soon as the pups can fly — in practice, late summer. South Carolina has no statute fixing the dates; SCDNR guidance is to avoid exclusions while young bats are flightless, and we follow it, because sealing a colony in June traps pups inside and fails anyway. What we do in June is confirm the colony, map every entry on those layered rooflines, and schedule the exclusion for when the window is right — then it is complete, all entries sealed at once, so the colony cannot simply shift to its second gap.

Summerville.wildlife_intro:
Our crew works Summerville from the Flowertown historic district and the pine-canopy subdivisions toward the Ashley swamps. The homes here sit in explosive Charleston suburban growth at Summerville against Edisto and Ashley river swamp and pine flatwoods, and that habitat explains most of what we find: raccoons, gray squirrels, armadillos, opossums account for the bulk of our Summerville calls, moving between the wild ground and the housing along the same creeks, field edges, and canopy streets every night.

Historic homes in Summerville's Flowertown, large new subdivisions under pine canopy, and older small-town homes upcounty, many with crawlspaces. In spring we handle denning raccoons and squirrels before litters grow, in summer the calls shift to bats, skunks, and digging animals in the yards, and in fall we seal homes ahead of the winter push. Every Summerville job starts with a full inspection of the roofline, foundation, and crawlspace, and ends with the entries sealed — because in Dorchester County there is always another animal nearby ready to use an open hole.

Summerville was built in a pine forest and has never left it. Charleston's planters came here to escape the Lowcountry summer fevers, and the town they made — the Flowertown, famous for its azaleas — still stands under one of the densest town canopies in South Carolina. That canopy is the wildlife story: gray squirrels and raccoons move through Summerville's historic district roof to roof without touching the ground, bats work the tall attics of the Victorian and early-1900s homes, and the pines drop the cones and resin scent that advertise every soffit gap. In the historic core, an animal in the attic is rarely a visitor; it is a resident of the forest the town is inside.

The growth tells the second story. Summerville has spread for forty years — subdivision on subdivision across Dorchester County — and the new streets stand where the pine woods stood last decade. Their animals are the displaced ones: raccoons testing new construction, armadillos and moles in lawns laid over forest floor, snakes along the new pond edges. Old Summerville's work is canopy and attic; new Summerville's is boundary and ground. Our inspections run both reads, because most addresses here sit inside one story and back onto the other.
Summerville.extendedBody:
Flowertown's canopy and the historic attic

Summerville's historic homes reward a complete read. The rooflines are layered — porches, additions, and sleeping porches joined across a century — and the canopy overhangs most of them, which makes every junction both an entry and a bridge endpoint. Squirrels chew in at the junctions; bats take the fascia gaps of the tall gables; raccoons use the failures both species leave. We seal in metal fitted to the old framing, cap the chimneys, and map the canopy contacts for your tree crew. On bat work we follow SCDNR's guidance rather than a fixed ban — South Carolina has no codified maternity blackout — which means avoiding exclusions while pups are flightless (roughly the early-summer weeks) as practice, and excluding completely, every gap at once, when the timing is right.

How this work is authorized in South Carolina

South Carolina does not license wildlife control operators — SCDNR keeps a referral list, nothing more — so any company claiming to be "SCDNR-licensed" is inventing a credential. The real instrument is the depredation permit under S.C. Code §50-11-2570(A): free, issued for the property and species, valid thirty days (a year for beaver). That permit is the legal basis for removal on your land, and it carries the state's handling rules with it — including that rabies-suspect animals are a public-health matter, reported through SC DPH. When you hire for this work in Summerville, the permit is the paper to ask about.

New streets, old woods

In the growth areas, the pattern is first-year and boundary work: displaced raccoons in new attics, armadillos and moles in new lawns, snakes along the fresh retention ponds. A perimeter inspection on a wooded-edge lot in its first year is the cheapest wildlife work in the county — it closes entries before the first colony, not after.

faqs.q: There is a dead animal smell in my St. George walls. What should I do?
faqs.a: Call us rather than opening walls at random. Our crew locates the carcass — a dead raccoon, opossum, or squirrel in a wall void or crawlspace is the usual source — removes it, and sanitizes the area. Carcasses of raccoons, skunks, and bats are handled with rabies precautions in line with Department of Public Health guidance, and we check how the animal got in so the entry is sealed as part of the same visit.

faqs.q: Something is digging up my St. George lawn at night and it smells like skunk. What is going on?
faqs.a: That combination is a striped skunk hunting grubs — the small cone-shaped holes across a lawn are its signature — and a den under a porch, deck, or crawlspace edge is usually nearby. Skunks are South Carolina's number-two rabies carrier in Department of Public Health testing, and routine relocation is against state law, so our crew traps calmly at the den with covered traps, handles the animal under SCDNR depredation rules, and screens the den opening so the next skunk finds it closed.

faqs.q: I saw a snake near my Harleyville home. Should I be worried?
faqs.a: Most snakes our crew is called about here are harmless rat snakes, black racers, and garter snakes following rodents and frogs. The ones that change the call are the copperhead, which is statewide, and — only in the wet coastal and swamp country — the cottonmouth. We identify first, from a safe distance: keep kids and pets inside, do not try to move or kill it, and tell us where it went. The southern hognose snake of the Sandhills is State Threatened and is never handled as a removal job, and venomous snakes are safety-and-referral work, not a guaranteed capture.

faqs.q: Beavers keep damming the branch behind our Ridgeville farm. Is one removal enough?
faqs.a: Usually it is the start, not the end — and South Carolina law is built for that honesty. Beaver depredation permits run a full year (most species get thirty days), because a dammed reach stays attractive to travelling beavers. We remove the animals working your reach, deal with the dam and the water level, and the permit window lets us follow through across the season rather than re-starting the paperwork per visit. Swamp-edge land in the Edisto drainage is beaver habitat permanently; the goal is your reach kept clear, and that is a manageable, honest goal.

faqs.q: A company told us they are SCDNR-licensed. Should we check anything else?
faqs.a: Start with that claim — it cannot be true. South Carolina issues no wildlife-control-operator license; SCDNR keeps a referral list, which is a listing, not a credential. What you can ask for is the working instrument: the depredation permit for your property under §50-11-2570(A), naming the species. Any operator doing removal should be arranging that permit as part of the job, and should be able to explain the state's handling rules — including that a rabies-suspect animal goes to SC DPH reporting. Those answers tell you more than a logo.

Ridgeville is Summerville's rural opposite number — a small Dorchester County town set in pine woods and farmland along the old highway, with Givhans Ferry State Park and the Edisto River a few miles west. Its wildlife work is the unhurried rural version: raccoons in the farmhouse chimneys and barn lofts, groundhogs in the field banks, skunks under the porches, bats in the older homes, and beavers working the creeks and swamp branches that cross the low ground toward the Edisto. Nobody in Ridgeville is surprised by an animal on the property; the calls come when the animal moves into the buildings.

The farmstead pattern rules here as it does across the rural Lowcountry: house, barns, well house, and equipment sheds share one animal population. A raccoon evicted from a Ridgeville attic without a look at the barn has been given a shorter commute, not a solution. Our inspections survey the whole parcel in one pass — which, in a community where the next neighbour is a quarter-mile off, is also simply how the economics of distance work.
Ridgeville.extendedBody:
The Edisto swamps and the ground work

Ridgeville's ground calls run wet. The branches draining to the Edisto flood their bottoms in wet years, and beavers dam them — backing water over field edges, drives, and the low farm roads. Beaver removal runs on the long depredation permit: under S.C. Code §50-11-2570(A), beaver permits run a full year rather than the usual thirty days, a recognition written into South Carolina law that beaver management is a season, not a visit. We treat a reach whole — animals, dam, and water level — and the year-long permit is what makes honest follow-through possible.

No license exists — here is what does

South Carolina does not license wildlife operators; SCDNR maintains a referral list only. Be skeptical of any company advertising itself as state-licensed for this work. The lawful instrument is the depredation permit issued for your property, and that is how our Ridgeville work runs: the permit names the species and the land, and the state's handling rules — including SC DPH reporting for rabies-suspect animals — come with it. Bats need no permit here, and exclusions follow SCDNR's guidance on timing: no sealing while pups are flightless, complete sealing when the season allows.

Farmstead sealing

Ridgeville's older homes and barns are sealed the rural way: caps on the chimneys, hardware cloth and metal at the loft and crawlspace openings, and the porch voids closed. Done parcel-wide in one programme, it is the difference between a farmstead that hosts wildlife in its fields and one that hosts it in its buildings.

faqs.q: Why do squirrels keep getting into Reevesville attics?
faqs.a: Gray squirrels need an opening little more than an inch wide, and the usual doors here are soffit corners, gable vents, and the gaps where additions meet the main roof, reached from fences and overhanging limbs. Trapping without sealing just invites the next squirrel, so our crew fits one-way doors, lets the animals leave, and seals every opening in steel — timed so a nursing litter is never sealed inside.
